newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Swiss govt pulls brakes on growing deficit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss govt pulls brakes on growing deficit.

text.p: The Swiss government, shocked by a projected 50 percent jump in next year's federal budget deficit, called on Monday for rigorous spending cuts and a constitutional amendment to control the budget by 2001.
"I am going to present shocking numbers today," Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger told reporters when presenting the bad news after a cabinet meeting in the capital of Berne.

Villiger's ministry said an initial tally of ministries' 1998 spending plans yielded a deficit of 8.7 billion francs ($6 billion), 50 percent wider than the 5.7 billion shortfall this year and another rise from 4.4 billion in 1996.
This was in sharp contrast with the government's goal of slashing annual deficits, which started mounting in 1991, to two percent of revenues or around one billion francs in 2001.

The Swiss federal budget has less of a market impact than those in other industrialised countries because of the relatively large volume of spending by the 26 cantons (states) and half-cantons and hundreds of local authorities.

But Villiger said the state was gradually losing its room to manoeuvre as a rising flow of money went to interest payments on the federal debt of nearly 90 billion francs, a quarter of gross domestic product, in 1997.
"We pay a million (Swiss francs) per hour every eight-hour day, or three and a half billion a year," he said.

To fortify its budget-balancing goals, the cabinet also approved a proposed anti-deficit amendment to the constitution, passing it to parliament for consideration in its autumn session. Voters have to approve it in a referendum next year.
The amendment would force Berne by law to meet an interim deficit cap of four billion francs in 1999 and a final target of two percent of revenue in 2001.
The cabinet said in a statement it had instructed Villiger to come up with spending cuts to bring the 1998 deficit down to between 6.5 billion and 7.0 billion francs.
It said the 1998 cuts would be considered after the July summer break, in time for the government's final draft budget to be presented to parliament in autumn.

Even after trimming the 1998 budget and passing planned reforms to shore up financing for state jobless insurance, projected deficits from 1999 through 2001 must be reduced by at least another two billion francs a year, the government said.
Based on current assumptions, deficits would range from 7.9 billion francs in 1999 to 6.0 billion in 2001.
Villiger said spending cuts would be targeted first of all at the biggest items on the federal budget -- social welfare, agriculture, transportation and the military.
He said rising deficits were caused by more than just an ongoing recession since 1991, the longest ever in Europe's slowest-growing economy.

Structural problems in the budget also had to be cleared up, including the division of tax revenues between the federal government and the cantons, he said. Berne would seek talks on this with the local authorities.
